name: Max Headroom signal hijacking
title: Two Chicago Stations Hijacked in One Night. Nobody Was Caught.
claims: Two Chicago TV stations were hijacked on November 22, 1987, about two hours apart by unidentified perpetrators | 1
The first hijacking hit WGN-TV's nightly newscast during the sports segment, about 9:14 p.m. | 1
WGN screens went black about 15 seconds before the masked figure appeared | 1
The figure wore a Max Headroom mask and sunglasses and rocked in front of a rotating corrugated metal panel mimicking the show's background | 1, 2
The only sound in the WGN hijacking was a garbled, buzzing noise | 1, 2
The WGN interruption was described as nearly 17 seconds, about 30 seconds, and half a minute in different accounts | 1, 2
WGN engineers ended it by changing the frequency of the studio-to-transmitter link (transmitter atop the John Hancock Center) | 1
Another account says WGN neutralized it by switching to an alternate transmitter | 2
The WGN sports anchor said "Well, if you're wondering what's happened, so am I" and joked the computer had "took off and went wild" | 1, 2
The anchor then resumed his report on the Chicago Bears game | 1
Max Headroom had a recently canceled TV show and appeared in soft drink advertisements | 2
The second hijacking hit WTTW, a PBS station, during Doctor Who serial Horror of Fang Rock, part one | 1, 2
The WTTW intrusion was at about 11:20 p.m. (one account) or 11:15 p.m. (another) | 1, 2
The WTTW broadcast included distorted audio, moans and laughter | 1, 2
The WTTW interruption lasted about 90 seconds | 1
The figure called a WGN sportscaster a "frickin' liberal" | 1, 2
The figure held up a can of Pepsi and referenced "Catch the wave," a slogan from an ad campaign featuring the real Max Headroom | 1, 2
The figure hummed the theme to the 1959 animated series Clutch Cargo and said "I still see the X!", a line sometimes misheard as "I stole CBS" | 1
The figure claimed to have made a "giant masterpiece" for "Greatest World Newspaper nerds"; WGN's call letters stand for "World's Greatest Newspaper" | 1, 2
The figure put on a glove and said his brother "had the other one" | 1, 2
A woman in a French maid costume, apparently masked, hit the figure with a flyswatter before the signal faded to static | 1
The unworn mask was briefly held in view and the figure cried out "Oh no, they're coming to get me! Ah, make it stop!" | 1
WTTW's transmitter was at the Sears Tower with no engineers on duty, and technicians could not counteract the takeover | 1, 2
A WTTW spokesman said technicians "attempted to take corrective measures, but couldn't" and that by the time they looked into it, it was over | 1
An air director recalled being increasingly stressed about their inability to do anything as the content got weirder | 1
The pirate broadcast ended when the hijackers ended it | 1
WTTW received numerous calls from viewers, some complaining about nudity | 1, 2
One viewer said on TV he got so upset he wanted to bust the TV set | 2
The method was sending a stronger microwave signal to the towers than the stations were sending, causing a capture effect | 1
Experts said it required extensive technical expertise and significant transmitting power, and the source was likely within line of sight of both towers atop tall downtown Chicago buildings | 1
Investigators thought the person beamed from an adjacent rooftop or had access to a powerful ground-based transmitter | 2
Some experts said suitable equipment could be bought for about $25,000 or rented for a few thousand dollars and moved in a few large suitcases | 2
The FCC investigated and could not find those responsible; the FBI also investigated per one account | 1, 2
An FCC official was quoted saying perpetrators faced a maximum fine of $100,000 and up to a year in prison; another account gives a $10,000 maximum | 1, 2
Investigators abandoned the manhunts without learning who, how or why | 2
The five-year statute of limitations expired in 1992 | 1, 2

Captain Midnight replaced HBO's signal with a complaint about prices the previous year; earlier in 1987 the Playboy Channel was hijacked; both offenders had clear motives and were located and prosecuted | 2
No one has ever claimed responsibility | 1
Speculation centers on an inside job by a disgruntled employee or former employee of WGN, or Chicago's underground hacker community | 1
The Max Headroom show was set in a future ruled by TV corporations where freedom fighters hijacked broadcasts, and the commentary was not lost on investigators | 2
A writer suggested the intrusion might be a proof-of-concept or have meaning not immediately evident | 2
WMAQ-TV inserted clips of the hijacking into a newscast; its sports anchor said "A lot of people thought it was real" and they got calls | 1
Motherboard called it an influential "cyberpunk hacking trope" | 1
It is referenced in an episode of Space Ghost Coast to Coast | 1
No other complete hijacking of a US commercial broadcast has occurred since | 2
Replication became almost impossible after the 2009 analog-to-digital switch | 1
A reader comment speculated the WTTW attack was a crime of opportunity (flagged as speculation) | 2
